query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy protective coatings, well‐engineered semi‐coherent phase boundaries serve as effective obstacles to dislocation climb and glide under continuous loading, thereby elevating the creep activation energy and stress exponent and reducing the steady-state creep rate.
generation.material_initial_state: A protective coating based on a dual-phase high-entropy alloy with an as-deposited mix of FCC and BCC phases exhibiting typical (i.e., not optimized) interphase boundary structures.
generation.intervention: Tailor the interphase boundary coherency by applying a controlled post-deposition thermal treatment or a slight composition adjustment aimed at enhancing the structural order and coherency at the FCC/BCC interfaces. This creates a set of coatings with enhanced semi‐coherent boundaries versus a control set with standard interphase boundary structures.
generation.conditions: Continuous loading creep tests at intermediate temperatures (approximately 500–600 °C) under service-relevant stress levels, which mimic the real operating conditions of protective coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherency and local strain fields at the FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced semi‐coherent boundaries impose local stress fields that impede the climb and glide of dislocations and delay or modify dynamic recrystallization. This results in an increased activation energy for creep and a higher stress exponent, as dislocation motion is more effectively pinned at the coherent interfaces compared to less coherent or disordered boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coatings with typical interphase boundaries, those with optimized semi-coherent interfaces will display a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate, alongside higher measured stress exponents and activation energies. Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) should verify the improved coherency at the FCC/BCC interfaces.
generation.baseline: Protective coatings produced by conventional deposition processes that lead to a mixture of FCC and BCC phases with randomly structured, less coherent interphase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate under sustained, moderate-to-high stress conditions at temperatures where dislocation-mediated creep (including climb and glide) is the primary deformation mechanism. At very high temperatures or at lower stresses where diffusion creep predominates, the effect of interface coherency may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis integrates dynamic recrystallization and precipitate effects identified in an FCC HEA (PMC7512559) with the role of interfacial barrier effects from molecular dynamics simulations in high-entropy superalloys (PMC12842692). The extension to protective coatings assumes that the same interphase coherency will yield similar dislocation blocking in a dual-phase FCC/BCC system, but scale effects and coating-specific microstructural features introduce uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of identical dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy coatings; one group is subjected to a controlled thermal treatment or minor composition adjustment to enhance the coherency of the FCC/BCC interphase boundaries while the other group remains as-deposited (control). Conduct systematic uniaxial creep tests at 500–600 °C under constant, service-relevant stresses and perform detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., using TEM) to assess interphase boundary structure.
measurements: Quantitative TEM/EDS metrics of interphase boundary coherency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with enhanced interphase coherency do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in creep resistance (i.e., lower strain rates, higher stress exponents, and higher activation energies) and if microstructural characterization does not confirm increased interface coherency relative to the control group, then the hypothesis that semi‐coherent boundaries effectively impede dislocation motion and enhance creep resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Stress Dependence of the Stress Exponent n and Creep Mechanism
cited_evidence.text: The steady-state creep behavior of alloys is typically described using the Bird–Dorn–Mukherjee equation []: where ε˙ represents the steady-state creep strain rate, A is a dimensionless constant, D0 is the diffusion coefficient, G is the shear modulus, ΔQ is the activation energy, kB is the Boltzmann constant, T is the absolute temperature, σ is the applied stress, n is the stress exponent, p is the grain size exponent, b is the Burgers vector, and d is the grain size. Among these parameters, the stress exponent n plays a critical role in identifying the governing creep mechanism [,]. Values of n ≈ 1–2 are typically associated with diffusion-controlled creep, whereas larger values (n > 3) indicate dislocation-mediated creep, and even higher values may reflect more complex mechanisms such as dislocation climb or stress-assisted phase transformation. Therefore, variations in n with applied stress provide a mechanistic indicator of stress-induced transitions in the dominant creep deformation mode. cited_evidence.text: As has been reported, the internal stress at the phase boundary intensifies with increasing |δ|, elevating the interfacial energy and promoting a morphological transformation of the precipitated γ′ phase from ellipsoidal to cubic [,,]. This transformation is driven by the misfit-induced strain energy, with δ serving as a key indicator of morphological stability. In general, a cubic morphology minimizes the alloy’s strain energy and enhances precipitate stability. However, when the value of |δ| becomes excessively large, the interfacial stress rises sharply, destabilizing the phase morphology and degrading creep resistance. This accounts for the observed non-monotonic relationship between |δ| and creep life. The intermediate-temperature creep behavior and microstructural evolution of CoCrFeNiMn HEA have been studied. Optical micrographs and TEM images of the dislocation substructure after creep deformation revealed the effects of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation on the deformation mechanisms. The following conclusions can be drawn:An obvious transition in stress exponent and average activation energy was observed: At low stresses, the values were approximately 5 to 6 and 268 kJ/mol, whereas at high-stress regions, the corresponding values were 8.9–14 and 380 kJ/mol. Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion is suggested as a possible rate-dominating mechanism at low stresses.At high stresses, obvious dynamic recrystallization occurred, leading to the refinement of average grain size. Simultaneously, nano-sized M23C6 carbides and the Cr-rich tetragonal σ phase were dynamically precipitated. High density of tangled and curved dislocation substructures was observed. In service, one of the essential design criteria for engineering components is the time-dependent deformation behavior (i.e., creep resistance). Macroscopic bulk compression or tension [,,], micro-pillar compression [,], and nano-indentation technique [,,,,,,] have been used to investigate the deformation behavior of materials in a wide range of length scales. Major discrepancies between the data obtained by nano-indentation and via conventional creep testing (i.e., compression/tension) have been reported [,]. This may be due to the complex multi-axial and inhomogeneous stress below indenters in comparison with uniaxial and homogeneous stress during bulk compression/tension test []. Despite these discrepancies, nano-indentation has been used as a convenient and fast approach to characterize the time-dependent deformation behavior at the small-scale for pure metals [,], bulk metallic glasses [,], and HEAs [,,,,,,,]. Most nano-indentation creep studies are limited to room temperature, low load (<100 mN), and face-centered cubic (FCC) metals/alloys [,,,,,,].
